lm.name: Infrastructure - Lone Star
lm.note: Texas’s nickname is the Lone Star State. You can see the Texas star on the state’s flag. Many Texans use the star as a decoration on gates, for example.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Maine Roadlines
lm.note: Maine often uses a dashed single yellow line or a combination of dashed and solid instead of a solid double one in the middle of a road. I feel like Maine does it a bit more often than other states in the region.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Maryland Overpass Code
lm.note: Some Interstate bridges in Maryland (but not the neighboring states or DC) seem to have this code painted on them. (Discovered by bagaboiebailey in the USA GeoGuessr Community server).

lm.name: Infrastructure - Midwest Grainy Roads
lm.note: Some rural roads in the Upper Midwest use a similar road pavement to Texas. They will have a grainy, ‘salt and pepper’-like road surface, but will vary in colour. These roads are most common in the state of Illinois.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Mile Marker
lm.note: California doesn’t use mile markers.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Minnesota Bridge Sign
lm.note: In Minnesota, these yellow signs with vertical, black triangles are placed before bridges at most major river crossings and at the beginnings and ends of guardrail sections on large highways.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Minnesota Stop Sign
lm.note: On most rural ‘stop’ signposts in Minnesota, a black-and-white marker is attached to the posts horizontally. The shape may vary slightly.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Nashville Bins
lm.note: Nashville has trash bins with the recognizable logo.

lm.name: Infrastructure - National Parks
lm.note:
Guardrails, signs, and signposts are commonly painted a medium brown colour in US National Parks, which are often located in the west. Guardrails that are painted brown can be made out of both wood and metal. Rock walls can also sometimes be seen in place of guardrails.

NOTE: There are occasional exceptions to this rule, so consider other clues before guessing in a National Park.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Nevada Bollard
lm.note: This bollard is found in Nevada. It consists of a reflector on a thin stick. The reflector is a vertical rectangle that consists of a white field surrounded by a black outline.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Nevada Mile Marker
lm.note: Top part has the highway name. The middle part is an abbreviation of the county name. The lower part has the mile number.

lm.name: Infrastructure - New Hampshire Interstate Sign
lm.note: These signs should only be found in NH (notice the dividing line between the two numbers).

lm.name: Infrastructure - New Hampshire US Route Sign
lm.note: These are also specific to New Hampshire. Notice the dividing line on the sign.

lm.name: Infrastructure - New Jersey - 500 Series County Routes
lm.note: These county routes are given unique three-digit numbers that begin with a 5. There is only one route per number. The same number cannot be duplicated in multiple counties. There is therefore only one County Route 525 in the entire state of New Jersey. What’s also interesting about the 500 Series routes is that they follow the same cardinal direction rule as Interstates: even-numbered routes run east-to-west and odd-numbered ones north-to-south. In common with the U.S. Routes, the numbers increase southward.

lm.name: Infrastructure - New Orleans Circle
lm.note: This circular windshield sticker is found in New Orleans, Louisiana.

lm.name: Infrastructure - No Middle Line
lm.note:
Some small roads in California lack a middle yellow line; instead only feature solid white lines on each side of the road.

NOTE: This can rarely be seen in other states.

lm.name: Infrastructure - North Carolina - Circular Pay to Park
lm.note: Raleigh, NC uses circular pay to park signs to indicate parking meter locations. (unlike Charlotte, NC)

lm.name: Infrastructure - North Carolina / Blue Parking Sign
lm.note: Charlotte uses green parking signs, whereas Raleigh uses blue parking signs.

lm.name: Infrastructure - North Carolina / Green Parking Sign
lm.note: Charlotte uses green parking signs, whereas Raleigh uses blue parking signs.

lm.name: Infrastructure - North Carolina / Streetcar
lm.note: Charlotte has a streetcar system unlike Raleigh.

lm.name: Infrastructure - North Carolina Signpost
lm.note: White signs attached to signposts can commonly be seen in North Carolina.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Number + Direction Road
lm.note:
Streets in Utah and Idaho, particularly in urban areas, are often named by using a combination of a number and cardinal direction (i.e. ‘600 South.’)

NOTE: This style of street naming can be found rarely in other Western states.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Oak Streetsign
lm.note: Oakland has this tree on their street name signs.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Oil Pumpjack
lm.note: Oil pumpjacks are short, industrial-looking metal structures located at the surface of oil fields and are used to pump crude oil from the earth below. They are most common in western states, particularly in Texas, Eastern New Mexico, and North Dakota.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Oklahoma Stopsigns
lm.note: In Oklahoma, you can often find a green rectangular sign with 3 rows of numbers attached to the back of stop signs at rural intersections

lm.name: Infrastructure - Overpass Milemarker
lm.note: In Alabama, overpasses have these mile markers hanging from them.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Parish
lm.note: Louisiana doesn’t call its counties counties but uses the word parish instead. This is a relic of the French colonial past of the state. You might occasionally spot the word on an intersection sign, for example. The location is guaranteed to be in Louisiana because no other state uses the word parish in that way.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Pennsylvania Intersection Signs
lm.note: Rectangular white signs can sometimes be seen attached to signposts at intersections in Pennsylvania. On top, the number of the converging state route is written.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Pillar Stripes
lm.note: Alabama likes to glue these stripes to overpass support pillars.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Pittsburgh Bridges
lm.note: Many bridges are used to connect the various neighbourhoods of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. These expansive, steel bridges are commonly painted bright yellow. Additionally, Pittsburgh is easy to identify because of it being flanked by 3 rivers and steep bluffs on all sides.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Pittsburgh Reflectors
lm.note: These circular reflectors are found in Pittsburgh.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Postal Marker
lm.note: Instead of Mile Markers, California uses postal markers that are white instead of green and have a county abbreviation.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Property Markers
lm.note:
A horizontal blue, red, or green sign can commonly be seen at the ends of driveways in Wisconsin and the Michigan peninsula. The house number is present, in addition to either the town name and or the road name (usually.)

NOTE: Nearby states often use similar markers, but typically lack any town or street name information and only feature numbers.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Rectangular Reflector
lm.note: These rectangular raised pavement markers are found in the south and west of the US and also in Massachusetts.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Red Streetsign
lm.note: Mesa, a city next to Phoenix, sometimes uses these red street name signs in the western part of the city.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Roadname on Sidewalk
lm.note:
In San Francisco, CA, almost every intersection has the road name written on the sidewalk.

This is due to the many earthquakes in this city, making sure every road is still labeled in case the streetsigns fall off.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Rock Walls
lm.note:
In rural areas of Connecticut, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire, short rock walls are commonly visible adjacent to the road.

NOTE: These rock walls can be found rarely in adjacent states.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Small Circle Bollard
lm.note: Roadside bollards in Wyoming often feature a dark metal pole with a white circular reflector at the top. The top of the metal pole is sometimes painted white or grey, which is unique to Wyoming.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Small Green Signs
lm.note:
Vermont features small rectangular green signs on stop sign posts with three rows of horizontal numbers. The top row of numbers correlates to the highway or road number that the road with the stop sign intersects with.

The State of New York uses similar style signs. However, these signs can be attached to different types of sign posts (town entry signs, highway signs, etc.)

lm.name: Infrastructure - South Carolina Intersection Signs
lm.note: Black street signs with white text can commonly be found at intersections in South Carolina.

lm.name: Infrastructure - SPEED Sign
lm.note: Speed signs in Oregon often simply have the word ‘Speed’ instead of the standard ‘Speed Limit’.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Square Guardrail
lm.note:
Square guardrails are the most dominant (but not the only) type of guardrail in the states of New York and Wyoming. They have a long bar across the top, with several square legs supporting them.

NOTE: These guardrails can be found, to a lesser extent, in some adjacent states.

lm.name: Landscape - Appalachian/Southern Hybrid
lm.note: Tennessee and Kentucky look like a mix of Appalachian and Southern Landscape.

lm.name: Landscape - Appalachians
lm.note:
The Appalachian mountain range is a low mountain range that runs through the eastern states. The general landscape consists of low, forested mountains, with beech and oak trees being a common sight.

NOTE: Houses in the south generally have less storeys. New England architecture, commonly consisting of wood panelling, high roofs and a porch, is also more common toward the north, especially in New England.

lm.name: Landscape - Badlands
lm.note: Badlands National Park features these distinct, sand-brown, eroded rock formations. The formations may sometimes appear more rounded, and lighter in colour.

lm.name: Landscape - Big Bend National Park
lm.note: Big Bend National Park is located along the Mexico border in Southwest Texas. It can be identified by its dry, rocky peaks and shrubby foliage. This park is adjacent to the Chihauhan desert, so plants such as yucca and prickly pear cactus are common.

lm.name: Landscape - Black Hills
lm.note:
The Black Hills, located in far Western South Dakota and far Eastern Wyoming, are a series of moderately tall mountains with large amounts of conifer trees and rocky outcroppings. The surrounding areas are typically much flatter with lesser tree cover.

NOTE: This area has a similar appearance to many areas within the Rocky Mountains, which lie further to the West.

lm.name: Landscape - Canadian Landscape (Maine)
lm.note: Landscapes vary quite a bit in New England. Maine in particular can look a lot like Canada.

lm.name: Landscape - Central Appalachians
lm.note: In the Appalachian area stretching from southern New York to southern Virginia, there are a lot of forest-covered rolling hills, with flat valleys dividing them. A majority of the ridges are oriented Southwest to Northeast.

lm.name: Landscape - Central Florida
lm.note: The soil gets a little more sandy in Central Florida. There are also more pine trees than palms (they’re occasionally seen too).

lm.name: Landscape - Central Valley
lm.note:
Central Valley, California can be recognized by its Mediterranean climate. This is reflected in its agriculture, seen in the vineyards and olive trees that can commonly be found here.

In addition, rolling hills can be seen toward the edges of the valley.

lm.name: Landscape - Circular Lakes
lm.note: Small circular shallow lakes are especially common in Central Florida around Lakeland and Orlando.

lm.name: Landscape - Colorado Ridge
lm.note: Central Colorado is home to a large North-to-South oriented mountain ridge. This divides the Rocky Mountains to the west and the Great Plains to the east.These mountains are adjacent to the major metropolitan areas of Boulder, Denver, and Colorado Springs.

lm.name: Landscape - Death Valley
lm.note:
Death Valley National Park can be easily recognized by the dry, sandy, treeless mountains that can be seen from the roads that go through the park. In Generation 3 coverage, the sky can look particularly dusty.

NOTE: Many smaller roads in Death Valley only have Generation 1 coverage.

lm.name: Landscape - Devil's Tower
lm.note: In far Northeastern Wyoming lies Devil’s Tower, which is a very tall, standalone butte protruding from the surrounding land. This can sometimes be seen from many miles away because of the lack of nearby mountains.

lm.name: Landscape - Driftless Area
lm.note: The driftless area in Southwestern Wisconsin is quite unique. It has features of Midwestern States (for example agriculture), but is very hilly.

lm.name: Landscape - Everglades
lm.note: Deep South Florida, between the metropolitan areas of Ft. Myers and Miami, features dense, jungle-like forests that have few inhabitants. Roads through these areas are commonly very straight and long.

lm.name: Landscape - Florida Jungle
lm.note: Deep South Florida, between the metropolitan areas of Ft. Myers and Miami, features dense, jungle-like forests that have few inhabitants. Roads through these areas are commonly very straight and long.

lm.name: Landscape - Florida Keys
lm.note:
The Florida Keys are an archipelago of tropical islands west of Miami. The highway connecting the islands can be recognized by green, tropical vegetation on the sides of the usually single lane road. The soil is also sandy white.

Urban locations are also similar, but with many more planted palm trees and mowed grass being a common sight.

lm.name: Landscape - Glacier National Park
lm.note:
Along the Canadian border in Montana lies Glacier National Park. It is easily recognizable by its extremely tall and steep mountain peaks. Most coverage is also hazy and taken during summer.

NOTE: Other National Parks within the Rocky Mountain range of the US can have a similar appearance, so consider other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Landscape - Great Basin
lm.note: The Great Basin, centred around Nevada, can be recognized by the tall, sometimes snow-capped mountains in the background. There are dry, but grassy, and slightly shrubby plains leading up to the mountains.

lm.name: Landscape - Great Basin - Green
lm.note: Within the Great Basin, greener mountains can be seen in Idaho and central Utah.

lm.name: Landscape - Great Basin - Oregon
lm.note: Within the Great Basin, more gradual, rocky hills can be seen in Oregon.

lm.name: Landscape - Great Plains
lm.note: The Great Plains are in the middle of the United States and stretch from the Canadian border in the North, to central Texas in the South. This area is primarily flat with few trees. Some areas feature agriculture fields, while others feature dry and barren grassy fields.

lm.name: Landscape - Guadaloupe Foothills
lm.note: In adjacent areas of New Mexico and Texas, smaller foothills of the Guadaloupe Mountains can be seen with relatively flat tops and shrubby foliage.

lm.name: Landscape - Guadalupe Mountains
lm.note: Along the New Mexico and or Texas border there is a ridge of tall, dry peaks known as the Guadalupe Mountains. In adjacent areas of both states, smaller foothills of these mountains can be seen with relatively flat tops and shrubby foliage.

lm.name: Landscape - Louisiana
lm.note: Flat and marshy landscapes are a common sight in Louisiana.

lm.name: Landscape - Lush Spruce Forest
lm.note: Spruce and pine forests are a common sight in the western United States in New Mexico, Colorado, Wyoming, Montana, and to the west of those states. The lush spruce forest types shown become increasingly common near the Pacific coast in Washington, Oregon, and California.

lm.name: Landscape - Mid-Atlantic Agricultural
lm.note: Some locations in the Mid-Atlantic region can look deceivingly Midwestern but with more trees.

lm.name: Landscape - Mid-Atlantic Forest
lm.note: Upstate New York and Pennsylvania are quite forested. Rolling hills are also common.

lm.name: Landscape - Mississippi River Valley
lm.note: The Lower Mississippi River Valley is a very flat and open landscape with red soil in areas of Tennessee, Arkansas, Mississippi, and Northeast Louisiana. Corn and other crops are common in this area.

lm.name: Landscape - Nebraska Sandhills
lm.note: The Nebraska Sandhills are a recognizable region of rolling hills covered with prairie grass in the central-north part of the state.

lm.name: Landscape - New England
lm.note: Landscapes vary quite a bit in New England. Maine in particular can look a lot like Canada if you know your countries in GeoGuessr. The topography of New England is mostly rolling hills. The forests are littered with fir trees and aspens.

lm.name: Landscape - Northern California
lm.note: One thing that sets NoCal apart from SoCal is the amount of palm trees. You generally see palms everywhere in the LA area but hardly any in the San Francisco Bay Area.

lm.name: Landscape - Northern Florida
lm.note: North Florida has sandier soil and rarely has any palm trees. Most forests are pine forests and the vibes feel more like Florida’s neighbors to the north than Florida itself.

lm.name: Landscape - Oklahoma Peaks
lm.note: Southwestern Oklahoma features a small area of rocky, shrubby peaks. Some of the mountains are also covered in trees, and the rocks can have a pinkish red tint to them.

lm.name: Landscape - Ouachita Mountains
lm.note: The Ouachita Mountains stretch from Eastern Oklahoma into West-Central Arkansas. Unlike the nearby Ozark Mountains, these mountains are typically more steep in nature and easier to see from a distance.

lm.name: Landscape - Pacific Rainforest
lm.note:
Temperate rainforests are found in coastal areas of Washington, Oregon, and Northern California. These rainforests feature many broadleaf trees, large conifers, and ferns.

NOTE: These rainforests stretch north into coastal British Columbia and Southeast Alaska as well.

lm.name: Landscape - Pine Forest Hills
lm.note: Spruce and pine forests are a common sight in the western United States in New Mexico, Colorado, Wyoming, Montana, and to the west of those states. The landscape that you can see in the picture meanwhile can be found in the states of Colorado, Montana, Wyoming, Utah, New Mexico, Arizona, Idaho, some locations in Nevada, and the eastern portions of Oregon, Washington, and California.

lm.name: Landscape - Prairie Pothole
lm.note: The area spanning from the Montana Border with Saskatchewan to the Western Great Lakes features many ‘prairie potholes.’ These are areas of low-lying wetlands that feature marshy grasses and small, shallow ponds.

lm.name: Landscape - Reddish Soil
lm.note:
You’ll find red soil everywhere in the South. The area where red soil can be found stretches all the way from some parts of Louisiana and Arkansas all the way to southern Virginia through Mississippi, southern Tennessee, Alabama, Georgia, South Carolina, and North Carolina.

The Oklahoma City region in Oklahoma is also notable for its red soil.

lm.name: Landscape - Rio Grande Valley
lm.note: The Rio Grande Valley in South Texas is extremely flat and features shrubby trees and agricultural fields. This area borders the Mexican state of Tamaulipas.

lm.name: Landscape - Rocky Mountains
lm.note: The area stretching from the Canadian border to Northern New Mexico is home to the Rocky Mountains. These jagged, rocky formations often feature many pine trees and visible snow all-year round at the highest peaks. Some areas of the Rocky Mountain Range are noticeably dry, with few trees.

lm.name: Landscape - Rolling Hills in Florida
lm.note: The area between the cities of Orlando and Lakeland in Florida sometimes feature low, rolling hills. Lakes and agricultural fields are also common in this area. This is the only main hilly area in central or southern Florida.

lm.name: Landscape - Roosevelt National Park
lm.note:
Theodore Roosevelt National Park features similar, sand-brown, eroded rock formations to Badlands National Park. The rock formations in this park tend to have more trees on them. Additionally, almost all coverage has fall colours visible.

NOTE: Similar formations can be seen in far eastern Montana as well.

lm.name: Landscape - Rural New Jersey
lm.note: Rural New Jersey looks strikingly southern.

lm.name: Landscape - Shiprock
lm.note: Shiprock is a rock formation and a municipality in northwestern New Mexico. This striking, isolated mountain is visible from distances of up to 40 km (roughly the red square) and is therefore a good clue for identifying the region within the Navajo Nation. Similar rock formations can be seen around Shiprock, but they do not have a long, low stone wall next to them.

lm.name: Landscape - South Florida
lm.note: South Florida is marshy and tropical. You’ll see an abundance of palm trees here.

lm.name: Landscape - Southern California - Rural
lm.note: Southern California outside the major cities of Los Angeles and San Diego is a barren desert.

lm.name: Landscape - Southern California - Urban
lm.note: In general Los Angeles and San Diego feel more tropical and the houses are more spread out as opposed to the more compact and dense feel of San Francisco.

lm.name: Landscape - Spruce/Pine Forest
lm.note: Spruce and pine forests are a common sight in the western United States in New Mexico, Colorado, Wyoming, Montana, and to the west of those states.

lm.name: Landscape - Tablelands
lm.note: The Southwest, centred around the Four Corners region of Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado, feature many mesas and tablelands. Often, these rock formations will be red in colour. Additionally, red soil is common in these areas.

lm.name: Landscape - Texas Hills
lm.note: Just west of the metropolitan areas of Austin and San Antonio Texas lies a large area of dry, rocky hills featuring many yucca and prickly pear plants. Texas Live Oak trees are the predominant tree type in this area.

lm.name: Language - Cherokee
lm.note: The Cherokee language is concentrated in the Cherokee Nation of Oklahoma and a few areas of North Carolina. It has a distinctive writing system called the Cherokee syllabary.

lm.name: Language - Finnish Roadnames
lm.note: In the town of Hancock in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, the street name signs are in Finnish as well as English.

lm.name: Language - Navajo
lm.note: Navajo is spoken in the Navajo Nation in Arizona and New Mexico. It’s the largest Native American language by the number of speakers. Navajo can be recognized from the double vowels and diacritics.

lm.name: Language - Spanish
lm.note: Spanish is the most commonly spoken non-English language in the United States. It’s the most prevalent near Mexico in Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California and in Florida where it’s the most spoken language in Miami-Dade County.

lm.name: Language - Town Suffix: -kill
lm.note: The ending -kill is common in New York place names. Examples include Catskill and Cobleskill. The word is derived from the Middle Dutch word kille (modern Dutch kil). As New York used to be under Dutch rule in the 17th century, that’s where you’ll find them the most.

lm.name: Misc - Aldi
lm.note: Aldi is found in the eastern half, starting at ~Mid Texas. It is however not found in Maine. In the West, it's only found in California and around Phoenix, Arizona.

lm.name: Misc - BP
lm.note:
BP is not found

  • In the West (starting at Kansas)
  • Louisiana, Arkansas
  • Upstate New York to Maine

lm.name: Misc - Buc-ee's
lm.note:
‘Buc-ee’s’ is a small chain of oversized gas stations located primarily in the state of Texas. These stores feature multiple rows of gas pumps, and a very large convenience store building.

NOTE: Some other nearby states have Buc-ee’s locations, but they are quite rare outside of Texas.

lm.name: Misc - Carl's Jr.
lm.note: ‘Carl’s Jr.’ and ‘Hardee’s’ are fast food restaurants that are operated by the same company and have a similar logo and colour scheme. However, Carl’s Jr. locations are all located on the West Coast and Southwest US, while Hardee’s are found in the central and Eastern areas of the country. Two states, Wyoming and Oklahoma, have both kinds of restaurants present.

lm.name: Misc - Casey's
lm.note: ‘Casey’s’ is a popular gas station and convenience store chain that is found in the Midwest, Plains, and parts of the Mid-South. Illinois, Iowa, and Missouri have the highest number of locations.

lm.name: Misc - Dunkin' Donuts
lm.note: Dunkin Donut's is not found in States Northwest of South Dakota.

lm.name: Misc - Food Lion
lm.note: Food Lion is mostly found between Maryland and South Carolina. You can sometimes see locations in Tennessee, Georgia and West Virginia.

lm.name: Misc - H-E-B
lm.note: ‘H-E-B’ is a supermarket that is only located in the state of Texas. Most H-E-B stores are in large cities.

lm.name: Misc - Hardee's
lm.note: ‘Carl’s Jr.’ and ‘Hardee’s’ are fast food restaurants that are operated by the same company and have a similar logo and colour scheme. However, Carl’s Jr. locations are all located on the West Coast and Southwest US, while Hardee’s are found in the central and Eastern areas of the country. Two states, Wyoming and Oklahoma, have both kinds of restaurants present.

lm.name: Misc - Hy-Vee
lm.note: ‘Hy-Vee’ is a supermarket that is common primarily in the Upper Midwest states of Iowa, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Illinois.

lm.name: Misc - In-N-Out Burger
lm.note: ‘In-N-Out Burger’ is a regional fast food chain located primarily in the Southwest US. California has the most locations.

lm.name: Misc - Kroger
lm.note:
Kroger is not found in

  • Nebraska to Minnesota
  • Pennsylvania or Northeast of it
  • Florida
  • Oklahoma

lm.name: Misc - Kum & Go
lm.note: ‘Kum & Go’ is a regional gas station chain based out of the state of Iowa. They also have pockets of locations in the Ozarks, Colorado, Wyoming, and North Dakota.

lm.name: Misc - Kwik Star
lm.note: ‘Kwik Star' is a chain of gas stations and convenience stores that are located in Iowa

lm.name: Misc - Kwik Trip
lm.note: ‘Kwik Trip’ is a chain of gas stations and convenience stores that are located in the Upper Midwest states of Wisconsin and Minnesota.

lm.name: Misc - Piggly Wiggly
lm.note: The supermarket chain ‘Piggly Wiggly’ is found mostly in the Southeast, as well as the state of Wisconsin.

lm.name: Misc - Pizza Ranch
lm.note: ‘Pizza Ranch’ is a restaurant chain that is found in the middle of the country. Iowa and Minnesota have the highest number of locations.

lm.name: Misc - Publix
lm.note: ‘Publix’ is a regional supermarket chain that has locations primarily in Florida and adjacent areas of the Deep South.

lm.name: Misc - Sheetz
lm.note: Another regional gas station and convenience store chain in the Eastern US is called ‘Sheetz’. Most of their locations are in the Mid-Atlantic and Central Appalachian areas of the US. Pennsylvania has the highest number of locations.

lm.name: Misc - Shoprite
lm.note: ‘Shoprite’ is a regional supermarket chain that has locations in 6 states in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic region of the US; Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, and Maryland.

lm.name: Misc - Stop-N-Go
lm.note: ‘Stop-N-Go’ is a chain of gas stations and convenience stores that are located in the Upper Midwest states of Iowa, Wisconsin and Minnesota.

lm.name: Misc - Tim Horton's
lm.note: ‘Tim Hortons’ is known for being the most popular restaurant chain in Canada. However, there are also many locations in the United States. They are primarily located in states adjacent to the Canadian Provinces of Ontario and Quebec, with a few locations also in Texas and Georgia.

lm.name: Misc - Waffle House
lm.note: The restaurant chain ‘Waffle House’ is a regional chain that is primarily found in the Southern and Southeast US. Some midwest and mid-atlantic states have some locations. Georgia, by far, is the state with the most Waffle House locations.

lm.name: Misc - WaWa
lm.note: ‘WaWa’ is a regional gas station and convenience store chain with locations in the Mid-Atlantic states and Florida. New Jersey and the Philadelphia, Pennsylvania area have the highest density of locations.

lm.name: Misc - Whataburger
lm.note: ‘Whataburger’ is a hamburger restaurant with locations across the South Central US. The State that is home to the most locations, by far, is Texas.

lm.name: Misc - Zaxby's
lm.note: ‘Zaxby’s,’ a fast-food chicken chain, is another restaurant that is most common in the Southeast US. There are several pockets outside the Southeast that have locations, such as Utah and Montana. Like Waffle House, Georgia has the highest number of locations.

lm.name: Trekker - Disney World Trekker
lm.note: GeoGuessr’s official maps have a bias for trekkers. Thus, if you’re playing the official US map or official state streaks, you should be aware of there being a lot of trekker coverage in Disney World in Orlando.

lm.name: Trekker - Dry Tortugas
lm.note:
The main island of Dry Tortugas National Park, west of Key West, can be identified by the hexagonal brick structure and the surrounding moat.

The Loggerhead Lighthouse, situated on the Loggerhead Key, has a brown top-half and a white bottom. The path on which the trekker walks on is also made of bright concrete, and many palm trees can be seen around the lighthouse.

lm.name: Vegetation - Balsam Fir
lm.note:
The Balsam Fir is a very symmetric tree. It has pretty dark needles and often grows close to the ground.

Within the US, you will find it in the Northeast, starting in Northern New York. You can also see it near the Great Lakes, on Latitudes similar to Vermont/Maine.

lm.name: Vegetation - Buckeye
lm.note:
You may already know Ohio’s nickname, the Buckeye State, but despite the name, buckeyes grow in other states too. They’re most commonly seen in the east from Ohio down through West Virginia, Virginia, and Kentucky to Tennessee and North Carolina. Some can be found in Missouri too.

California is the only state in the west where you can see buckeyes.

lm.name: Vegetation - Cabbage Palmetto
lm.note: Sabal palmetto is native to the subtropical coastal regions of the American states of Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, southeastern North Carolina, and extreme southern Texas.

lm.name: Vegetation - California Fan Palm
lm.note: Washingtonia filifera is the only palm native to the Western United States and one of the country's largest native palms.

lm.name: Vegetation - Dormant Grass
lm.note: Grass that is used in lawns in the southern US (colloquially known as Bermuda and St. Augustine grasses) go dormant in the winter months. This causes the lawns to turn beige or light brown in winter; whereas grasses used in more northern areas of the US stay much greener in winter.

lm.name: Vegetation - Douglas Fir
lm.note:
Extremely tall conifer trees (Douglas firs) with a dark brown bark, and dark green leaves, can most commonly be seen in Cascadia. Notably, they can also be found in northern California, Idaho and as far east as Montana.

Beware that they are also commonly found in British Columbia.

lm.name: Vegetation - Gumbo Limbo Tree
lm.note: The Gumbo Limbo tree can be recognized by its red bark and by its irregular, sometimes twisting trunks. Its leaves are green and oval shaved. You will only find it in Coastal Florida, south of Orlando and south of Tampa.

lm.name: Vegetation - Palms
lm.note: Palm trees are common in coastal areas of the Southeastern states, as well as the Desert Southwest region. Shown here is the Mexican Fan Palm, which is most common in California and along the Gulf Coast, but other palm tree types have a similar range.

lm.name: Vegetation - Quaking Aspen
lm.note: Aspen trees are thin trees with white barks that often grow in groups. In the contiguous states, you can find it in North-East USA, all states that border the great lakes (+NE-Iowa), in Northern Idaho and in random areas in the West.

lm.name: Vegetation - Sagebrush
lm.note: Great Basin Sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata) is a short, shrubby blue-green bush that is common in the interior western United States.It is most common in arid areas.

lm.name: Vegetation - Saguaro
lm.note: Saguaro cacti are most commonly shaped like tall, straight tubes with several branches extending from the main tube. They are most commonly found in southern Arizona, on the Sonoran border.

lm.name: Vegetation - Saw Palmetto
lm.note: Saw Palmetto grows in clumps or dense thickets in sandy coastal areas, and as undergrowth in pine woods or hardwood hammocks. You can find it in coastal areas of Florida and Georgia.

lm.name: Vegetation - Southern Live Oak
lm.note: This tree can commonly be found in Florida and along the southern coast as shown by the range map. A southern live oak will often have Spanish moss hanging from the branches, giving the tree a pendulous appearance.

lm.name: Vegetation - Southern Magnolia
lm.note: This tree can only be found in the South. However, southern magnolias don’t grow in southern Florida. The range stretches from Orlando and Tampa to North Carolina and Texas.

lm.name: Vegetation - Southern Pines
lm.note: The loblolly pine (Pinus taeda), and longleaf pine (Pinus palustris), commonly referred to as southern pines in the community, are found throughout the southeastern US. They are a great way to recognize this region, as they are abundant, recognizable and mostly limited to this part of the country. They tend to be tall, with fluffy-looking clusters of pine needles.

lm.name: Vegetation - Spanish Moss
lm.note: Spanish moss, appearing as greyish white drapes, can sometimes be seen on trees in the deep south.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: No Passing Zone
lm.note: • Triangular yellow signs with the phrase ‘No Passing Zone’ are exclusive to the US.
