lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• The US uses yellow middle lines and white outer lines.
  • Double middle lines are the most common.
  • On divided roads, the outer line closest to the median will be yellow, and the other lines will usually be white.

--- NOTE:

  • Double middle lines are less common in Canada, but not rare – use this meta with caution.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: Rumble Strips
lm.note:
• Interstate highways, US highways, and some state roads have rumble strips in each edge of the road; which are small indentations in the pavement perpendicular to the road.

--- NOTE:

  • Rumble strips may appear in Canada, but are much more rare.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: Speed Limit
lm.note:
• The US uses the phrase ‘Speed Limit’ on their speed signs.

--- NOTE:

  • Canada uses the word ‘Maximum’ on their speed signs.

lm.name: Idaho/Utah Bollard
lm.note: This thin bollard with a small white reflector at the top is unique to Utah and Idaho

lm.name: Montana/South Dakota Bollard
lm.note:
The most common type of roadside bollard in South Dakota and Montana features a dark metal post with a white diamond on each side of the top.

NOTE: These bollards can be found to a lesser extent in other western states.

lm.name: Nevada Bollard
lm.note: This bollard is found in Nevada. It consists of a reflector on a thin stick. The reflector is a vertical rectangle that consists of a white field surrounded by a black outline.

lm.name: Oregon Bollard
lm.note: This bollard is unique to Oregon state in US.

lm.name: Washington Bollard
lm.note: The state of Washington uses bollards that consist of a white or brown post with a white rectangle on the front of the bollard, and two smaller white or silver squares on the back of the bollard.

lm.name: Western Bollards
lm.note:
These bollards are found in the upper western states from Utah to Washington.

  • The white version is more common in Washington, Oregon and Idaho

  • The green version is more common in Montana, Idaho and Utah

  • The black version is more common in Wyoming, Utah, South Dakota and colorado

NOTE: Technically, all colors can be found in every western state, but the likelihood of finding them is higher in the states listed.

lm.name: Wyoming Bollard
lm.note: Roadside bollards in Wyoming often feature a dark metal pole with a white circular reflector at the top. The top of the metal pole is sometimes painted white or grey, which is unique to Wyoming

lm.name: Appalachians
lm.note:
The Appalachian mountain range is a low mountain range that runs through the eastern states. The general landscape consists of low, forested mountains, with beech and oak trees being a common sight.

NOTE: Houses in the south generally have less storeys. New England architecture, commonly consisting of wood panelling, high roofs and a porch, is also more common toward the north, especially in New England.

lm.name: Badlands National Park
lm.note: Badlands National Park features these distinct, sand-brown, eroded rock formations. The formations may sometimes appear more rounded, and lighter in colour.

lm.name: Big Bend National Park
lm.note: Big Bend National Park is located along the Mexico border in Southwest Texas. It can be identified by its dry, rocky peaks and shrubby foliage. This park is adjacent to the Chihauhan desert, so plants such as yucca and prickly pear cactus are common. The roads in the national park are covered in Generation 3.

lm.name: California Central Valley
lm.note: Central Valley, California can be recognized by its Mediterranean climate. This is reflected in its agriculture, seen in the vineyards and olive trees that can commonly be found here. In addition, rolling hills can be seen toward the edges of the valley.

lm.name: Central Appalachians
lm.note: In the Appalachian area stretching from southern New York to southern Virginia, there are a lot of forest-covered rolling hills, with flat valleys dividing them. A majority of the ridges are oriented Southwest to Northeast.

lm.name: Central Colorado Ridge
lm.note: Central Colorado is home to a large North-to-South oriented mountain ridge. This divides the Rocky Mountains to the west and the Great Plains to the east. These mountains are adjacent to the major metropolitan areas of Boulder, Denver, and Colorado Springs.

lm.name: Coastal Maui
lm.note: Coastal areas of Maui are noticeably more lush and green. Banana plants, palm trees, and views of the mountains are all common.

lm.name: Death Valley National Park
lm.note:
Death Valley National Park can be easily recognized by the dry, sandy, treeless mountains that can be seen from the roads that go through the park. In Generation 3 coverage, the sky can look particularly dusty.

NOTE: Many smaller roads in Death Valley only have Generation 1 coverage.

lm.name: Devils Tower
lm.note: In far Northeastern Wyoming lies Devil’s Tower, which is a very tall, standalone butte protruding from the surrounding land. This can sometimes be seen from many miles away because of the lack of nearby mountains.

lm.name: Florida Low Hills
lm.note: The area between the cities of Orlando and Lakeland in Florida sometimes feature low, rolling hills. Lakes and agricultural fields are also common in this area. This is the only main hilly area in central or southern Florida.

lm.name: Great Basin
lm.note: The Great Basin, centred around Nevada, can be recognized by the tall, sometimes snow-capped mountains in the background. There are dry, but grassy, and slightly shrubby plains leading up to the mountains. The tallest mountains are in Nevada, Utah and California. More gradual, rocky hills can be seen in Oregon, and greener mountains can be seen in Idaho and central Utah.

lm.name: Great Plains
lm.note: The Great Plains are in the middle of the United States and stretch from the Canadian border in the North, to central Texas in the South. This area is primarily flat with few trees. Some areas feature agriculture fields, while others feature dry and barren grassy fields.

lm.name: Guadalupe Mountains
lm.note: Along the New Mexico and or Texas border there is a ridge of tall, dry peaks known as the Guadalupe Mountains. In adjacent areas of both states, smaller foothills of these mountains can be seen with relatively flat tops and shrubby foliage.

lm.name: Guam North
lm.note: Similarly, the northern half of the island is mostly flat.

lm.name: Guam South
lm.note: Hills are mostly found on the southern half of the island.

lm.name: Hawai’i Plains
lm.note: The Island of Hawai’i (also referred to as The Big Island) is both the largest and farthest southeast island with Street View coverage in the state. The interior areas feature rolling, grassy plains and volcanic rocks. You can typically see one or more of the island’s volcanoes from the road. Both Generation 3 and Generation 4 coverage are common in this area.

lm.name: Hawaiʻi Forests
lm.note:
Rural roads going through forests within a flat landscape are commonly found south of the city of Hilo, on the island of Hawaiʻi.

NOTE: Mountainous forests are dotted around Hawaii, but if you are in one, and you see red soil with Generation 3, consider guessing in Kauai, the westernmost covered island.

lm.name: Hawaii Red Hill
lm.note: The Red Hill can easily be recognised by this unique barren, red rocky landscape. Due to the high altitude, clouds are usually visible below you.

lm.name: Hawaiian Lattice
lm.note: The infamous “Hawaiian lattice” can be recognized by the volcanic soil and rocks that are abundant in the region. Volcanic vegetation can also be seen lining the roads. Note that the angle of the roads is a big clue for the area, and that this lattice was built on the slope of Mauna Loa.

lm.name: Kauai Landscape
lm.note:
The Island of Kauai is the furthest west island in Hawaii with official Google coverage. This island has deep red soil and has large rugged hills with lush, jungle-like vegetation. This island also has exclusively Generation 3 coverage.

NOTE: Other islands such as Maui and Molokaʻi have similar soil colours, but the hillsides on them will typically have less dense vegetation.

lm.name: Lānaʻi Central Region
lm.note: The Island of Lānaʻi is a small, yet distinct island that lies just south of Moloka’i. A volcano is found just east of the centre of the island, adjacent to the town of Lānaʻi. In this area, tall Cook pines are abundant. In addition, some main roads near the centre of the island are lined with younger Cook pines. The island only has Generation 3 coverage.

lm.name: Lānaʻi Coastal Hills
lm.note: Towards the coasts of the island of Lānaʻi, hills dotted with dry grass and shrubby vegetation are commonly seen. These areas are very rural with few buildings.

lm.name: Lower Mississippi River Valley
lm.note: The Lower Mississippi River Valley is a very flat and open landscape with red soil in areas of Tennessee, Arkansas, Mississippi, and Northeast Louisiana. Corn and other crops are common in this area.

lm.name: Maui Plains
lm.note: The Island of Maui sits southeast of Molokaʻi. In the centre of the island, you will find dry and somewhat flat grasslands with one or both of the mountain ranges on the island visible. Both Generation 3 and Generation 4 coverage are common on the island.

lm.name: Mesa Landscape
lm.note: The Southwest, centred around the Four Corners region of Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado, feature many mesas and tablelands. Often, these rock formations will be red in colour. Additionally, red soil is common in these areas.

lm.name: Molokaʻi Landscape
lm.note: The Island of Molokaʻi is just southeast of the Island of Oʻahu. This island features deep red soil, dry-looking vegetation, and a prominent volcano on the eastern end of the island. Molokaʻi is also very sparsely populated. This island only has Generation 3 coverage.

lm.name: Nebraska Sandhills
lm.note: The Nebraska Sandhills are a recognizable region of rolling hills covered with prairie grass in the central-north part of the state.

lm.name: Ouachita Mountains
lm.note: The Ouachita Mountains stretch from Eastern Oklahoma into West-Central Arkansas. Unlike the nearby Ozark Mountains, these mountains are typically more steep in nature and easier to see from a distance.

lm.name: Prairie Potholes
lm.note: The area spanning from the Montana Border with Saskatchewan to the Western Great Lakes features many ‘prairie potholes.’ These are areas of low-lying wetlands that feature marshy grasses and small, shallow ponds.

lm.name: Rio Grande Valley
lm.note: The Rio Grande Valley in South Texas is extremely flat and features shrubby trees and agricultural fields. This area borders the Mexican state of Tamaulipas.

lm.name: Rocky Mountains
lm.note: The area stretching from the Canadian border to Northern New Mexico is home to the Rocky Mountains. These jagged, rocky formations often feature many pine trees and visible snow all-year round at the highest peaks. Some areas of the Rocky Mountain Range are noticeably dry, with few trees.

lm.name: San Antonio Hills
lm.note: Just west of the metropolitan areas of Austin and San Antonio Texas lies a large area of dry, rocky hills featuring many yucca and prickly pear plants. Texas Live Oak trees are the predominant tree type in this area.

lm.name: South Florida Jungle
lm.note: Deep South Florida, between the metropolitan areas of Ft. Myers and Miami, features dense, jungle-like forests that have few inhabitants. Roads through these areas are commonly very straight and long.

lm.name: Theodore Roosevelt National Park
lm.note:
Theodore Roosevelt National Park features similar, sand-brown, eroded rock formations to Badlands National Park. The rock formations in this park tend to have more trees on them. Additionally, almost all coverage has fall colours visible.

NOTE: Similar formations can be seen in far eastern Montana as well.

lm.name: Tundra
lm.note: Most of interior and northern Alaska lies in subarctic or tundra climate zones. These areas feature relatively low amounts of forest undergrowth and shorter trees.

lm.name: Washington Golden Fields
lm.note:
Agricultural golden fields can commonly be seen in eastern Washington.

NOTE: Flat areas of northern and eastern Oregon can have a similar appearance.

lm.name: West Coast Rainforests
lm.note:
Temperate rainforests are found in coastal areas of Washington, Oregon, and Northern California. These rainforests feature many broadleaf trees, large conifers, and ferns.

NOTE: These rainforests stretch north into coastal British Columbia and Southeast Alaska as well.

lm.name: West Oklahoma Peaks
lm.note: Southwestern Oklahoma features a small area of rocky, shrubby peaks. Some of the mountains are also covered in trees, and the rocks can have a pinkish red tint to them.

lm.name: National Park Guardrail
lm.note:
Guardrails, signs, and signposts are commonly painted a medium brown colour in US National Parks, which are often located in the west. Guardrails that are painted brown can be made out of both wood and metal. Rock walls can also sometimes be seen in place of guardrails.

Here you can find a map showing where all US National Parks are located.

NOTE: There are occasional exceptions to this rule, so consider other clues before guessing in a National Park.

lm.name: NY & Wyoming Guardrail
lm.note:
Square guardrails are the most dominant (but not the only) type of guardrail in the states of New York and Wyoming. They have a long bar across the top, with several square legs supporting them.

NOTE: These guardrails can be found, to a lesser extent, in some adjacent states.

lm.name: Alaska-Fireweed-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Herbácea alta que coloniza claros y cunetas, formando manchas extensas de flores rosa-púrpura en espigas. El color intenso en masa es la pista principal. Muy común en: AK.

--

🇬🇧 Tall herb that colonizes clearings/roadsides, forming broad patches of pink-purple flowers in spikes. The intense color in large masses is the main clue. Found mainly in: AK.

lm.name: BigSageBrush-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Arbusto dominante de estepa, gris plateado, hojas muy pequeñas y mata redondeada (≈0,5–2 m), formando tapiz uniforme con mucho suelo visible. Más continuo que creosote. Principalmente en: ID, NV, UT, OR, WY.

--

🇬🇧 Dominant steppe shrub, silvery-gray, very small leaves and a rounded bush (≈0.5–2 m), forming a uniform carpet with lots of visible bare soil. More continuous than creosote. Found mainly in: ID, NV, UT, OR, WY.

lm.name: BlueOak-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Roble de copa abierta y “traslúcida”, follaje mate azul-verdoso/gris. Desde lejos parece más claro que otros robles. Tronco y ramas retorcidas con corteza gris pálida finamente escamosa.

--

🇬🇧 Oak with an open, “see-through” crown, dull blue-green/gray foliage. From far away it reads lighter than other oaks. Trunk and twisted limbs show pale gray, finely scaly bark.

lm.name: Bluestem+GramaGrass-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Pradera abierta dominada por macollas de bluestem y grama: penachos azul-verdosos en verano, textura de “pelo” al viento. Tapiz continuo sin arbustos; en otoño vira a paja/cobre con espigas ligeras.

--

🇬🇧 Open prairie dominated by bluestem and grama bunches: blue-green tufts in summer with a hair-like, wind-rippled texture. Continuous ground cover with few shrubs; in fall it turns straw/copper with seedheads

lm.name: CreosoteBush-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Arbusto redondeado verde-oliva con muchos tallos desde la base, muy espaciado y con suelo desnudo visible entre plantas. Más “bola” verde que sagebrush plateado. Se encuentra principalmente en: AZ, CA, NV.

--

🇬🇧 Rounded olive-green shrub with many stems from the base, widely spaced with bare ground between plants. Greener and more “ball-like” than silvery sagebrush. Found mainly in: AZ, CA, NV.

lm.name: Greasewood
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Matorral bajo y abierto con dos tonos: Atriplex forma matas redondeadas, densas y gris-plateadas. Sarcobatus aparece como arbusto erguido, ramas rígidas espinosas y follaje verde oscuro, creando mosaico bicolor.

--

🇬🇧 Low, open shrubland with two tones: Atriplex forms rounded, dense, silvery-gray mounds. Sarcobatus shows as an upright shrub with rigid spiny branching and dark-green foliage, creating a two-color mosaic.

lm.name: Magnolia-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Árbol perenne de hojas grandes, gruesas y muy brillantes, verde oscuro, dando aspecto “subtropical” suave. Se separa de robles/pinos por hojas anchas lustrosas. Se encuentra principalmente en: FL, LA, MS.

--

🇬🇧 Evergreen tree with large thick very glossy leaves, dark green, giving a soft “subtropical” look. Easy to spot vs oaks/pines thanks to broad shiny leaves. Found mainly in: FL, LA, MS.

lm.name: MojaveYucca-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Yucca con hojas largas en espada formando rosetas puntiagudas, a menudo sobre tronco, silueta muy “escultórica”. Se distingue por el penacho rígido y vertical. Se encuentra principalmente en: CA, NV.

--

🇬🇧 Yucca with long sword-like leaves in spiky rosettes, often on a trunk, with a very “sculptural” silhouette. Stands out by the stiff, vertical tuft. Found mainly in: CA, NV.

lm.name: OregonOak-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Roble de copa muy ancha y redondeada de presencia más “pesada”, ramas retorcidas y horizontales. Masa de hojas verde más oscura y tono más vivo (arriba puede verse algo brillante. Frente a coníferas, destaca por ramas desnudas en invierno. Principalmente: OR, WA y norte de CA; sobre todo OR.

--

🇬🇧 Oak with a very broad, rounded, “heavier” presence, with twisted, horizontal limbs. Leaf mass is darker green and more vivid (the upper surface can look slightly glossy). Compared to conifers, it stands out by bare branches in winter. Mainly: OR, WA, and northern CA; especially OR.

lm.name: RedSpruce-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Conífera cónica con aspecto más “erizado”, agujas rígidas y ramas algo colgantes, verde medio-oscuro. Se ve más áspera que abetos (Balsam fir) y menos abierta que pinos. Se encuentra principalmente en: ME, NH, NY.

--

🇬🇧 Conical conifer with a more “bristly” look, stiff needles and slightly drooping branchlets, medium-dark green. Rougher than firs and less open than pines. Found mainly in: ME, NH, NY.

lm.name: ShagbarkHickory-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Hickory es fácil de identificar si se ve cerca: corteza “deshilachada” en tiras largas colgantes, copa alta e irregular. Si el tronco parece peludo/rasgado, es la pista nº1. más frecuente y diverso en el Este.

--

🇬🇧 Hickory is easy to identify up close: “shaggy” bark peeling in long, hanging strips, with a tall, irregular crown. If the trunk looks furry or torn, that’s the #1 clue. It’s most common and most diverse in the eastern U.S.

lm.name: SilverCholla-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Cactus arbustivo con muchos “brazos” finos y aspecto plateado por espinas claras, formando bolas ramificadas. Se distingue de opuntias porque no tiene palas planas. Se encuentra principalmente en: CA, NV.

--

🇬🇧 Shrubby cactus with many thin “arms” and a silvery look from pale spines, forming branched rounded shapes. Unlike opuntias, it doesn’t have flat pads. Found mainly in: CA, NV.

lm.name: Sitka Spruce - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Mezcla muy densa de píceas y abetos: muchas copas cónicas apretadas, verde oscuro y aspecto uniforme, casi sin huecos. Más cerrado y sombrío que pinos abiertos. Se encuentra principalmente en: AK.

--

🇬🇧 Very dense spruce-and-fir mix: many tight conical crowns, dark green, and a uniform look with few gaps. More closed and shadowy than open pine stands. Found mainly in: AK.

lm.name: SugarMaple-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Caducifolio de copa amplia y bastante simétrica, textura uniforme, muy típico en mezcla de bosques del norte. Suele verse más “ordenado” que robles y puede dar colores intensos en otoño. Se encuentra principalmente en: MI, NH, NY, VT.

--

🇬🇧 Deciduous tree with a broad fairly symmetrical crown and uniform texture, very typical in northern mixed hardwoods. Often looks more “orderly” than oaks and can show strong fall color. Found mainly in: MI, NH, NY, VT.

lm.name: Washington-SubalpineFir-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Abeto muy estrecho y cónico (“aguja”), agujas planas verde-azuladas con reverso blanquecino/plateado y corteza gris lisa con ampollas de resina. A menudo forma masas densas y, en altura, se ve achaparrado. Se encuentra principalmente en: WA, OR, ID, MT, WY, UT, CO; también en: AK, CA (NW), NV (NE), AZ, NM.

--

🇬🇧 Very narrow, spire-shaped fir (“needle”), flat blue-green needles with a whitish/silvery underside and smooth gray bark with resin blisters. Often forms dense stands and can look stunted at higher elevations. Found mainly in: WA, OR, ID, MT, WY, UT, CO; also in: AK, CA (NW), NV (NE), AZ, NM.

lm.name: WesternYellowPine-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Pino siempreverde muy alto, tronco recto con corteza canela-anaranjada en grandes placas tipo puzzle. Copa alta, penachos de acículas largas. Suele formar pinares abiertos con troncos espaciados.

--

🇬🇧 Very tall evergreen pine with straight trunk and cinnamon-orange bark in big jigsaw-puzzle plates. High crown with tufts of long needles. Often forms open, park-like pine stands with spaced trunks.

lm.name: Wheatgrass-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Pradera de wheatgrass y needlegrass: tapiz verde uniforme de wheatgrass con penachos pajizos y aristas finas. Si aparece grama, se ve mosaico: parches azul-verdosos muy bajos entre macollas más altas.

--

🇬🇧 Wheatgrass–needlegrass prairie: uniform green wheatgrass carpet with straw-colored plumes and fine awns. If grama is present, it turns patchy: very low blue-green mats between taller bunches. Enlace: Foto de ejemplo (web): buscar “wheatgrass needlegrass prairie” y “grama grass shortgrass prairie”

lm.name: YellowBirch-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Abedul caducifolio de corteza amarillo-bronce que se pela en tiras finas, copa ligera y textura aireada. Contrasta con coníferas oscuras en bosques húmedos. Principalmente en: ME, NY, MI, VT, NH.

--

🇬🇧 Deciduous birch with yellow-bronze bark peeling in thin strips, a light crown and airy texture. Contrasts with dark conifers in moist forests. Found mainly in: ME, NY, MI, VT, NH.

lm.name: Agriculuture - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Grandes campos en hileras perfectas. Maíz forma “pared” alta verde en verano; soja es alfombra baja densa. Avena/cebada son más cortas, uniformes, y se vuelven doradas antes de cosecha.

--

🇬🇧 Large fields in perfectly straight rows. Corn makes a tall green “wall” in summer; soybeans read as a low, dense carpet. Oats/barley stay shorter, uniform, and turn golden before harvest.

lm.name: Canyon Live Oak - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Siempreverde de copa redondeada y muy densa; la masa foliar verde oscuro puede verse brillante. Se notan ramas gruesas y, a veces, varios troncos. Corteza gris-parda, escamosa y estrechamente agrietada.

--

🇬🇧 Evergreen with a rounded, very dense crown; the dark-green leaf mass can look glossy. Thick limbs stand out and, at times, multiple trunks. Bark is gray-brown, scaly, and narrowly furrowed.

lm.name: EasternHemlock - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Eastern Hemlock (Tsuga canadensis): conífera “plumosa” con punta caída. Vive en Noreste + Apalaches (valles/ríos frescos y húmedos). Conos pequeños. Vs Western (Tsuga heterophylla): Agujas: Eastern en 2 filas (peinado) / Western desordenadas (hetero). Contexto: Western con musgo/helechos y gigantes (Douglas-fir, redcedar, Sitka) / Eastern con mezcla de caducifolios.

🇬🇧 Eastern Hemlock (Tsuga canadensis): feathery conifer with a drooping leader. Northeast + Appalachians (cool, moist valleys/streams). Small cones. Vs Western (Tsuga heterophylla): Needles: Eastern two-ranked/flat / Western messy all around. Context: Western mossy giant forests (Douglas-fir, redcedar, Sitka) / Eastern mixed forests.

lm.name: Easterns-Oaks-Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Robles caducifolios del este en bosques mixtos: copas amplias y redondeadas crean dosel continuo. En invierno quedan ramas desnudas y gruesas. Troncos robustos con corteza gris, escamosa a profundamente agrietada.

--

🇬🇧 Eastern deciduous oaks in mixed forests: broad, rounded crowns form a continuous canopy. In winter, bare, thick limbs remain. Stout trunks show gray bark, from scaly plates to deep furrows.

lm.name: Giant Red Wood - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Coast Redwood / “Giant redwood” (Sequoia sempervirens): árboles altísimos en columnas rectas, corteza rojiza/marrón muy fibrosa (parece “cuerda” o “pelusa”), bosques húmedos con helechos, musgo y a veces niebla. Suele aparecer en la costa del norte de California (Humboldt/Del Norte) y a veces asoma hacia SW Oregon. Pista GeoGuessr: si ves un “pasillo” de troncos rectos gigantes + ambiente húmedo/verde oscuro, casi estás en el fog belt costero.

--

🇬🇧 Coast Redwood / “Giant redwood” (Sequoia sempervirens): extremely tall straight pillar-like trunks, reddish-brown very fibrous bark (ropey/shaggy look), wet forests with ferns, moss, and often foggy vibes. Mostly in Northern California’s coast (Humboldt/Del Norte), with some presence into SW Oregon. GeoGuessr cue: giant straight trunks forming a “corridor” + damp dark-green understory = coastal fog-belt redwoods.

lm.name: MojaveJoshuaTree - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Yucca arborescente con tronco leñoso y brazos gruesos tipo candelabro. En cada punta, rosetas densas de hojas rígidas y punzantes, formando “pompones” verdes. Silueta irregular, a veces con múltiples ramas.

--

🇬🇧 Tree-form yucca with a woody trunk and thick candelabra-like arms. At each tip, dense rosettes of stiff, sharp leaves form green “pom-poms.” Irregular silhouette, sometimes with multiple branches.

lm.name: MontereyCypress - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Monterey cypress (Cupressus / Hesperocyparis macrocarpa): conífera costera de follaje muy denso (hojas en escamas, no agujas), verde oscuro, que en zonas expuestas al mar adopta la silueta típica “vencida por el viento”: copa aplanada, ramas largas y dobladas en una dirección, como un paraguas horizontal. Es un “tell” clásico de costa ventosa y con niebla (California central/norte). Pista GeoGuessr: si ves cipreses con forma de bandera (todo empujado hacia un lado) en barrios o carreteras costeras, piensa California coast.

--

🇬🇧 Monterey cypress (Cupressus / Hesperocyparis macrocarpa): a coastal conifer with dense scale-like foliage (not needles), dark green, famous for its wind-sculpted look near the ocean: a flattened crown with branches bent/leant in one direction, like a sideways umbrella. A classic tell for windy, foggy coastal environments (central/northern California). GeoGuessr cue: cypresses shaped like a flag (all pushed one way) along coastal roads/neighborhoods → think California coast.

lm.name: RedPine - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Red Pine (Pinus resinosa): conífera del Norte de EE. UU. y Canadá, tronco recto y rojizo, copa abierta y aireada, con huecos entre ramas (aspecto algo “despeinado”). Común en bosques fríos y plantaciones del área Great Lakes.

--

🇬🇧 Red Pine (Pinus resinosa): Northern US & Canada conifer with a straight, reddish trunk and an open, airy crown with visible gaps. Common in cold forests and plantations of the Great Lakes region.

lm.name: SabalPalmetto - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Palmera de tronco único recto; a veces conserva “boots” en patrón espinoso, otras queda liso. Copa compacta de hojas en abanico con costa. Frondas secas colgantes si no se podan.

--

🇬🇧 Palm with a straight single trunk; sometimes it keeps spiky “boots”, other times it turns smooth. Compact crown of costapalmate fan leaves; dead fronds hang as an untrimmed skirt.

lm.name: SaguaroCactus - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Cactus columnar gigante de color verde-azulado, con costillas verticales marcadas y espinas finas. Con la edad forma brazos erguidos tipo candelabro; domina llanuras y laderas abiertas del Desierto de Sonora.

--

🇬🇧 Giant blue-green columnar cactus with strong vertical ribs and fine spines. With age it grows upright candelabra arms; it dominates open flats and slopes across the Sonoran Desert.

lm.name: SawPalmetto - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Palma baja casi sin tronco, formando matas redondeadas densas. Hojas rígidas en abanico, verdes a plateadas, crean un “mar” de rosetas; suele tapizar el sotobosque bajo pinares abiertos.

--

🇬🇧 Low, nearly trunkless palm forming dense rounded clumps. Stiff fan leaves, green to silvery, create a “sea” of rosettes; often carpets the understory beneath open pine flatwoods.

lm.name: SwordFern - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Helecho perenne en grandes matas radiales, frondes arqueadas y rígidas tipo espada (0,5–1,5 m), verde oscuro brillante. Cubre el sotobosque en parches densos bajo coníferas húmedas del Pacífico Noroeste.

--

🇬🇧 Evergreen fern in big radial clumps, stiff arching sword-like fronds (0.5–1.5 m), dark glossy green. Forms dense understory patches beneath moist conifers of the Pacific Northwest.

lm.name: Thatch Palm - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Palmera de tronco único delgado y gris, con cicatrices anilladas. Copa de abanicos circulares, puntas caídas y envés plateado. Nativa de Florida Keys; Más probable de encontrar en el sur de Florida y en urbano puede verse plantada por todo el estado con menos frecuencia.

--

🇬🇧 Slender single-trunk palm with a gray trunk and ringed leaf scars. Crown of circular fan leaves with drooping tips and a silvery underside. Native to the Florida Keys; planted ornamentally across Florida.

lm.name: TobosaGrass+BuffaloGrass+GramaGrass- Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Pastizal ralo con tobosa en macollas altas y tiesas, y gramas más bajas en parches. Arbustos dispersos. Común en Chihuahuan: Trans-Pecos (TX), sur de NM y SE de AZ.

--

🇬🇧 Open, thin-cover grassland with tall, stiff tobosa bunches and lower grama patches. Scattered shrubs. Common across the Chihuahuan: Trans-Pecos (TX), southern NM and southeastern AZ.

lm.name: WashingtoniaFilifera - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Palmera de tronco único grueso con “falda” de hojas secas colgantes. Copa de abanicos gris-verdosos con filamentos blancos. En oasis/manantiales forma palmerales; sin poda, la falda baja casi al suelo.

--

🇬🇧 Thick single-trunk palm with a hanging “skirt” of dead fronds. Crown of fan leaves with white thread-like filaments. In oases/springs it forms groves; untrimmed, the skirt drops near the ground.

lm.name: Wine - Veg
lm.note:
🇪🇸 Viñedo en hileras perfectas, plantas bajas/medias repetidas, con postes y alambres (espaldera) marcando líneas muy rectas. Suelo muy limpio entre filas; en invierno puede verse casi “solo sarmientos”. Principalmente en: CA, OR, WA; con más frecuencia en CA.

--

🇬🇧 Vineyard in perfectly straight rows, low/medium repeating vines, with posts and wires (trellises) creating very regular lines. Very clean soil between rows; in winter it can look like “bare canes.” Found mainly in: CA, OR, WA; most frequent in CA.

lm.name: Oklahoma City bait
lm.note: Around Lake Stanley Draper, basically downtown Oklahoma City, the landscape suddenly looks like Brazil or Kenya.

lm.name: Double Yellow
lm.note:
• The US uses yellow middle lines and white outer lines.
  • Double middle lines are the most common.

--- NOTE:

  • Double middle lines are less common in Canada, but not rare – use this meta with caution.

lm.name: Rumble Strips
lm.note:
• Interstate highways, US highways, and some state roads have rumble strips in each edge of the road.
  • These are small indentations in the pavement perpendicular to the road.
  • They can be located on the outside edges of the road and in between lanes on multi-lane highways.

--- NOTE:

  • Rumble strips may appear in Canada or Mexico, but are much more rare.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner
lm.name: Cali three stripes
lm.note: Utility poles with 3 yellow stripes are most commonly found in California.

lm.name: Alabama Pole Plates
lm.note: You can see these fine plates with a round part on the side on most poles in Alabama and I have never seen anything like this elsewhere.

lm.name: Alabama Vertical End of Guardrail
lm.note: Guardrails in Alabama feature vertical yellow and black patterns, distinguishing them from other southern states. Note: This only applies within the Southern states

lm.name: Alaska Northern Trees
lm.note: Trees in Alaska are generally thinner and have less broad leaves than those seen in the other 49 states.

lm.name: Appalachian Fence
lm.note:
Dark-coloured wooden fences with several horizontal wooden supports are common in farming areas of central and southern Appalachia, stretching from Pennsylvania to Georgia.

NOTE: These types of fences can be found elsewhere to a lesser extent, so use other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Appalachians
lm.note:
The Appalachian mountain range is a low mountain range that runs through the eastern states. The general landscape consists of low, forested mountains, with beech and oak trees being a common sight.

NOTE: Houses in the south generally have less storeys. New England architecture, commonly consisting of wood panelling, high roofs and a porch, is also more common toward the north, especially in New England.

lm.name: ATV Signs
lm.note: These green ATV Route signs are unique to Wisconsin.

lm.name: Black Tar
lm.note: A black stripe can sometimes be seen in between the two yellow, middle road lines in California.

lm.name: Brownstone Buildings
lm.note: Brownstone buildings are typically row houses or government buildings made out of various types of brick and sandstone. They are most commonly found in dense urban areas of the Northeast US, as well as Chicago.

lm.name: California Stripes
lm.note: Utility poles in California usually have markings at the bottom of the pole that consist of 3 yellow stripes.

lm.name: Canola
lm.note: Along the Canadian border in North Dakota, and rarely Montana, fields filled with short yellow canola flowers (Brassica napus) can commonly be seen from the road.

lm.name: Central Appalachians
lm.note: In the Appalachian area stretching from southern New York to southern Virginia, there are a lot of forest-covered rolling hills, with flat valleys dividing them. A majority of the ridges are oriented Southwest to Northeast.

lm.name: Central Valley
lm.note:
Central Valley, California can be recognized by its Mediterranean climate. This is reflected in its agriculture, seen in the vineyards and olive trees that can commonly be found here.

In addition, rolling hills can be seen toward the edges of the valley.

lm.name: Concrete Paving
lm.note:
Concrete paving on main highways is much more common in Iowa than in other states.

NOTE: Concrete paving on residential streets is commonly seen throughout the Midwest states and parts of the East Coast.

lm.name: Corn
lm.note:
Corn fields can most commonly be found in these regions:-Iowa

-North of Iowa

-Nebraska without NW

lm.name: Cotton
lm.note: Cotton is a crop that produces large fields of fluffy white flowers. It is most commonly produced in coastal Southeast States, the Lower Mississippi River Valley, Western Texas, and parts of California and Arizona.

lm.name: Diamond Bollard
lm.note:
The most common type of roadside bollard in South Dakota and Montana features a dark metal post with a white diamond on each side of the top.

NOTE: These bollards can be found to a lesser extent in other western states.

lm.name: Dormant Grass
lm.note: Grass that is used in lawns in the southern US (colloquially known as Bermuda and St. Augustine grasses) go dormant in the winter months. This causes the lawns to turn beige or light brown in winter; whereas grasses used in more northern areas of the US stay much greener in winter.

lm.name: Double Sign Posts
lm.note:
Signs attached to two signposts can be seen in Michigan. Not all signs are attached to two signposts.

NOTE: Double signposts can also be seen in other states, but are not as common.

lm.name: Douglas Fir
lm.note:
Extremely tall conifer trees (Douglas firs) with a dark brown bark, and dark green leaves, can most commonly be seen in Cascadia. Notably, they can also be found in northern California, Idaho and as far east as Montana.

Beware that they are also commonly found in British Columbia.

lm.name: Golden Fields
lm.note:
Agricultural golden fields can commonly be seen in eastern Washington.

NOTE: Flat areas of northern and eastern Oregon can have a similar appearance.

lm.name: Great Basin
lm.note: The Great Basin, centred around Nevada, can be recognized by the tall, sometimes snow-capped mountains in the background. There are dry, but grassy, and slightly shrubby plains leading up to the mountains.

lm.name: Great Basin - Green
lm.note: Within the Great Basin, greener mountains can be seen in Idaho and central Utah.

lm.name: Great Basin - Oregon
lm.note: Within the Great Basin, more gradual, rocky hills can be seen in Oregon.

lm.name: Great Plains
lm.note: The Great Plains are in the middle of the United States and stretch from the Canadian border in the North, to central Texas in the South. This area is primarily flat with few trees. Some areas feature agriculture fields, while others feature dry and barren grassy fields.

lm.name: Green Bollard
lm.note: Green bollards are common and (almost) unique to Idaho and Colorado, they exist in different forms, not only the one on this picture.

lm.name: Green/Red Rectangular Signs
lm.note:
Maine, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts use small green and red rectangular signs to mark the ends of bridges and guardrails.

NOTE: Not all bridges and guardrails in these states will have these markers.

lm.name: H-Reflector
lm.note: Snowplowable raised pavement markers can only be found on highways in the eastern states shown in the image. They are built into the road and somewhat resemble the letter H.

lm.name: Hanging Lights
lm.note:
Many large intersections in Michigan have stop lights and signs that hang from wires that stretch across the middle of the intersection. These markers are commonly in yellow boxes.

NOTE: These are not completely unique to Michigan, but are most commonly seen there

lm.name: Hawaii Antenna
lm.note:
A stubby antenna can be seen in most Generation 3 coverage on Hawaii.

NOTE: The antenna is not always visible, so make sure to look out for other clues before guessing. (This antenna can also be seen in Cambodia, New Zealand, and US National Parks)

lm.name: Hawaii Smallcam
lm.note: Hawaii also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front, with parts of the black car being visible. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.

lm.name: Hawaiian Place names
lm.note:
Hawaii is the only state to use its own language, though English is still predominantly used. Most place names are in Hawaiian, so you can spot it on street signs, and other road markers.

Hawaiian is a vowel-oriented language that only uses eight consonants: H, K, L, M, N, P, W, and (ʻ), called an ʻOkina.

Every Hawaiian word ends in one of 5 vowels: A, E, I, O, or U.

Each vowel can also have a macron over it: Ā, Ē, Ī, Ō, and Ū.

These vowels are often combined to make Diphthongs. I.e. UI, AI, AE, etc...

lm.name: Idaho Rectangular Bollard
lm.note: These bollards with a rectangle on top are common in Idaho and can only be seen there in western US. The rectangle can be white or yellow. Montana has a similar yellow version, but the reflector is much larger.

lm.name: Iowa Sidepost
lm.note: The signpost on the side, as shown below, is unique to the state of Iowa in the Plains and Midwest. (only applies if you are in the Plains or Midwest)

lm.name: Kansas Signpost Reflectors
lm.note: These white reflectors on signposts are unique to Kansas. They are most commonly seen on ‘stop’ signs in rural areas.

lm.name: Kentucky Thin Strips
lm.note: Kentucky commonly uses thin strips on the edge of the road, which is unique to the state. These strips are not to be confused with long thin strips that do not reach the edge of the road, which can also be used in Kentucky but also elsewhere.

lm.name: Large Center Line Gap
lm.note:
Yellow lines with a noticeably larger gap in between them are most common in Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Oregon. They can also be found to a lesser extent in Washington, Alabama, and Michigan.

NOTE: Wide middle lines can also rarely appear in other states, so consider other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Massachusetts Pole Plates
lm.note: These rectangular plates, which can be white or yellow, can be seen on the side of poles in eastern Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Connecticut. These plates can very rarely be seen elsewhere.

lm.name: Minnesota Bridge Marker
lm.note: In Minnesota, these yellow signs with vertical, black triangles are placed before bridges at most major river crossings and at the beginnings and ends of guardrail sections on large highways. (I have seen these in other states but they are upsidown)

lm.name: Minnesota Signpost reflectors
lm.note: On most rural ‘stop’ signposts in Minnesota, a black-and-white marker is attached to the posts horizontally. The shape may vary slightly.

lm.name: Mississippi River Valley
lm.note: The Lower Mississippi River Valley is a very flat and open landscape with red soil in areas of Tennessee, Arkansas, Mississippi, and Northeast Louisiana. Corn and other crops are common in this area.

lm.name: Nebraska Sandhills
lm.note: The Nebraska Sandhills are a recognizable region of rolling hills covered with prairie grass in the central-north part of the state.

lm.name: Nevada Bollard
lm.note: This bollard is found in Nevada. It consists of a reflector on a thin stick. The reflector is a vertical rectangle that consists of a white field surrounded by a black outline.

lm.name: New England Rock Walls
lm.note:
In rural areas of Connecticut, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire, short rock walls are commonly visible adjacent to the road.

NOTE: These rock walls can be found rarely in adjacent states.

lm.name: New England Shingled Walls
lm.note:
Houses in coastal New England often feature shingle walls, which are layered wood panels overlapping each other.

A similar style of panelling can also be seen, however, having a wider range than the one shown above.

lm.name: No Center Lines
lm.note:
Some small roads in California lack a middle yellow line; instead only feature solid white lines on each side of the road.

NOTE: This can rarely be seen in other states, notably Kentucky

lm.name: North Carolina Signpost white Signs
lm.note: White signs attached to signposts can commonly be seen in North Carolina.

lm.name: North Carolina Street Signs
lm.note:
North Carolina commonly uses a style of street signs showing street numbers and arrows in addition to the street name.

NOTE: Other states occasionally feature street signs with similar designs, so use other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Number/Direction Street Signs
lm.note:
Streets in Utah and Idaho, particularly in urban areas, are often named by using a combination of a number and cardinal direction (i.e. ‘600 South.’)

NOTE: This style of street naming can be found rarely in other Western states.

lm.name: Ohio Gap
lm.note: In Ohio, you can often see gaps in road lines where there is a RPM (raised pavement marker). It can also sometimes be seen elsewhere (Tennessee or New Jersey) but it is much rarer.

lm.name: Oil Pumpjack
lm.note: Oil pumpjacks are short, industrial-looking metal structures located at the surface of oil fields and are used to pump crude oil from the earth below. They are most common in western states, particularly in Texas, Eastern New Mexico, and North Dakota.

lm.name: Oklahoma Fence
lm.note: Red metallic fences are very common in Oklahoma and the surrounding states, particularly Kansas, Texas, and Arkansas. This is not 100% so look for other clues before sending.

lm.name: Oklahoma No Guardrail Reflectors
lm.note: Oklahoma has no guardrails with reflectors inside it. If you see a guardrail with reflectors, don’t guess Oklahoma.

lm.name: Oklahoma Stop Sign
lm.note: In Oklahoma, you can often find a green rectangular sign with 3 rows of numbers attached to the back of stop signs at rural intersections

lm.name: Oregon Bollard
lm.note: This bollard is extremely common in Oregon and is almost exclusive to this state. It can rarely be seen in California (but usually when it is the case, it is not exactly this bollard, the white rectangle will be bigger or it won’t be all the way on top for example).

lm.name: Oregon Roadlines
lm.note: These short and fine lines can often be seen in between Oregon roadlines which are usually wide, you can see similar lines elsewhere but it is useful to distinguish Oregon from surrounding states especially Washington who also often uses wide roadlines.

lm.name: Oregon Speed
lm.note: Speed signs in Oregon often simply have the word ‘Speed’ instead of the standard ‘Speed Limit’.

lm.name: Ouachita Mountains
lm.note: The Ouachita Mountains stretch from Eastern Oklahoma into West-Central Arkansas. Unlike the nearby Ozark Mountains, these mountains are typically more steep in nature and easier to see from a distance.

lm.name: PA Bollards
lm.note: Pennsylvania bollards are very common on guardrails and sometimes elsewhere. They can be white or yellow and are recognizable by their shape and black cap.

lm.name: PA Rectangular white signs
lm.note: Rectangular white signs can sometimes be seen attached to signposts at intersections in Pennsylvania. On top, the number of the converging state route is written.

lm.name: Pacific Rainforest
lm.note:
Temperate rainforests are found in coastal areas of Washington, Oregon, and Northern California. These rainforests feature many broadleaf trees, large conifers, and ferns.

NOTE: These rainforests stretch north into coastal British Columbia and Southeast Alaska as well.

lm.name: Prairie Pothole
lm.note: The area spanning from the Montana Border with Saskatchewan to the Western Great Lakes features many ‘prairie potholes.’ These are areas of low-lying wetlands that feature marshy grasses and small, shallow ponds.

lm.name: Publix
lm.note: ‘Publix’ is a regional supermarket chain that has locations primarily in Florida and adjacent areas of the Deep South.

lm.name: Pueblo Architecture
lm.note:
Pueblo Revival style houses are commonly seen in New Mexico. They are typically constructed of adobe or brick and concrete. They have rounded edges and flat roofs, and are usually sand-brown in colour.

NOTE: Pueblo style houses can also be seen in Arizona and Colorado to a lesser extent.

lm.name: Rectangular Reflector
lm.note: These rectangular raised pavement markers are found in the south and west of the US and also in Massachusetts.

lm.name: Reddish Soil
lm.note: Many parts of the Deep South, stretching from Oklahoma to South Carolina, have reddish soil. The exact tint of the soil can range from yellow to deep red.

lm.name: Rice
lm.note: Rice production only occurs in a few areas of the US, so it is very useful for region guessing. It is typically grown in large, flat fields that resemble low prairies. It is only grown in north-central California and the Lower Mississippi River Valley in Arkansas, Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi.

lm.name: Rio Grande Valley
lm.note: The Rio Grande Valley in South Texas is extremely flat and features shrubby trees and agricultural fields. This area borders the Mexican state of Tamaulipas.

lm.name: Rocky Mountains
lm.note: The area stretching from the Canadian border to Northern New Mexico is home to the Rocky Mountains. These jagged, rocky formations often feature many pine trees and visible snow all-year round at the highest peaks. Some areas of the Rocky Mountain Range are noticeably dry, with few trees.

lm.name: Sagebrush
lm.note: Great Basin Sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata) is a short, shrubby blue-green bush that is common in the interior western United States.It is most common in arid areas.

lm.name: Saguaro
lm.note: Saguaro cacti are most commonly shaped like tall, straight tubes with several branches extending from the main tube. They are most commonly found in southern Arizona, on the Sonoran border.

lm.name: SC Black Street Signs
lm.note: Black street signs with white text can commonly be found at intersections in South Carolina.

lm.name: SC Reflectors (No Roadlines)
lm.note: If you see a small road without roadlines that has Southern Reflectors in the middle, you will most likely be in South Carolina. In other states the reflectors will always be next to roadlines. Sometimes these roadlines can be faded so be careful.

lm.name: Shoprite
lm.note: ‘Shoprite’ is a regional supermarket chain that has locations in 6 states in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic region of the US; Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, and Maryland.

lm.name: Short Stilts
lm.note: Similar in style to aforementioned stilt houses, houses with much shorter stilts are common in the western and central Gulf Coast. These houses typically feature short stilts made of concrete or wood (1-3 feet off the ground) and are primarily found in areas near the coast and any adjacent rivers.

lm.name: Shotgun Houses
lm.note: Very narrow, one-storey houses made out of wood are called ‘shotgun houses.’ They are most common in and around New Orleans (LA,) Houston (TX,) Louisville (KY,) and the state of Mississippi.

lm.name: Sloped Roofs
lm.note: Buildings with very large, sloped roofs are most common in the states of Oklahoma, Texas, and Louisiana. They can also be seen in neighbouring states to a lesser extent.

lm.name: Southern Pines
lm.note: The loblolly pine (Pinus taeda), and longleaf pine (Pinus palustris), commonly referred to as southern pines in the community, are found throughout the southeastern US. They are a great way to recognize this region, as they are abundant, recognizable and mostly limited to this part of the country. They tend to be tall, with fluffy-looking clusters of pine needles.

lm.name: Soy
lm.note: Soybeans are short, dark green crops organised in long rows and are found in similar regions where corn is grown. They are most common in the Eastern Plains, Midwest, Lower Mississippi Valley, and areas of the Mid Atlantic.

lm.name: Spanish Colonial Revival
lm.note: Spanish Colonial Revival Architecture can be categorised as buildings with lightly-coloured stucco walls and red clay-tile roofs. They can be found in the desert southwest states of California, Nevada, Arizona, and Texas. You can also find similar types of buildings in Florida and coastal Georgia.

lm.name: Spanish Moss
lm.note: Spanish moss, appearing as greyish white drapes, can sometimes be seen on trees in the deep south.

lm.name: Square Guardrails
lm.note:
Square guardrails are the most dominant (but not the only) type of guardrail in the states of New York and Wyoming. They have a long bar across the top, with several square legs supporting them.

NOTE: These guardrails can be found, to a lesser extent, in some adjacent states.

lm.name: Stacked Triplexes
lm.note:
Older three story wooden houses, also called ‘stacked triplexes,’ are very common in urban areas of the Northeast. They are most prevalent in New York, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and Massachusetts.

NOTE: These types of houses are also somewhat common in cities in Atlantic Canada.

lm.name: Stilt Houses
lm.note: Stilt houses can sometimes be seen on the coast. These are especially common toward the south, and on the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.

lm.name: Tablelands
lm.note: The Southwest, centred around the Four Corners region of Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado, feature many mesas and tablelands. Often, these rock formations will be red in colour. Additionally, red soil is common in these areas.

lm.name: Texas Bands
lm.note:
Yellow or red bands can commonly be seen around signposts in Texas.

NOTE: Similar reflectors can sometimes be seen in other states, such as Hawaii.

lm.name: Texas Bumps
lm.note: These littles rectangular bumps on center lines are unique to Texas. You can see some round bumps in some other states but rectangular ones are only in Texas.

lm.name: Texas Guardrail Bollards
lm.note: White Bollard + Grey/Yellow Square. These bollards are unique to Texas on guardrails in the southern United States.

lm.name: Texas Hills
lm.note: Just west of the metropolitan areas of Austin and San Antonio Texas lies a large area of dry, rocky hills featuring many yucca and prickly pear plants. Texas Live Oak trees are the predominant tree type in this area.

lm.name: Texas Pavement
lm.note:
Texan roads often have a grainy, ‘salt and pepper’-like road surface.

NOTE: Similar pavement can sometimes be seen in adjacent states such as New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Colorado.

lm.name: Thick Center Lines
lm.note:
Some roads in West Virginia, Virginia, and Maryland use middle yellow lines that are thicker than traditional yellow road lines.

NOTE: These are not present on all roads in these states, and can be found elsewhere, so use this tip in conjunction with other clues.

lm.name: Utah Bollard
lm.note: This bollard is unique to Utah.

lm.name: Utah Idaho Bollard
lm.note: This type of bollard with a white square on top is unique to Utah and Idaho. If the square is not totally on top then it should be Idaho.

lm.name: Vermont Small Green Stop Signs
lm.note:
Vermont features small rectangular green signs on stop sign posts with three rows of horizontal numbers. The top row of numbers correlates to the highway or road number that the road with the stop sign intersects with. For example, this image is taken from Vermont State Road 116, looking towards the intersecting road.

The State of New York uses similar style signs. However, these signs can be attached to different types of sign posts (town entry signs, highway signs, etc.)

lm.name: Vertical House Numbers
lm.note:
Properties in rural and exurban Ohio, Lower Michigan, and Indiana commonly feature a vertically-oriented metal sign with white numbers, indicating the house number of the adjacent building. These signs are most commonly blue or green, and are commonly attached to mailboxes.

NOTE: These may be rarely found in other states.

lm.name: Virginia Rectangle white signs
lm.note: Rectangular white signs can sometimes be seen at intersections in Virginia.

lm.name: Washington Bollard
lm.note: The state of Washington uses bollards that consist of a white or brown post with a white rectangle on the front of the bollard, and two smaller white or silver squares on the back of the bollard.

lm.name: WI Bollard
lm.note: These simple white bollards with black reflectors are unique to Wisconsin.

lm.name: WI Property Markers
lm.note:
A horizontal blue, red, or green sign can commonly be seen at the ends of driveways in Wisconsin and the Michigan peninsula. The house number is present, in addition to either the town name and or the road name (usually.)

NOTE: Nearby states often use similar markers, but typically lack any town or street name information and only feature numbers.

lm.name: WI Warning Pole Plate
lm.note: A rectangular white metal plate, with an orange rectangle and diamond, can be seen on most poles in Wisconsin and the Michigan peninsula.

lm.name: WI/MO Letters
lm.note: Wisconsin and Missouri are the only two states that use a lettering system (A - ZZZ) for their county highways. Wisconsin signs typically have the word ‘county’ above the letter, while Missouri signs typically do not. The borders of the signs also vary slightly.

lm.name: Wyoming Bollard
lm.note: Roadside bollards in Wyoming often feature a dark metal pole with a white circular reflector at the top. The top of the metal pole is sometimes painted white or grey, which is unique to Wyoming.

lm.name: Yellow Posts
lm.note: Yellow posts like this one are common in Colorado and can be seen more rarely in Utah or Texas. It can rarely be seen in other states. (Very rare and not the most consistant; I have also seen it twice in Virginia)

lm.name: No passing zone sign
lm.note: Yellow triangular signs with the text "No Passing Zone" are unique to the United States.

lm.name: Speed limit signs
lm.note: U.S. speed limit signs feature the text "Speed Limit," while Canadian signs use the text "Maximum."

lm.name: Minnesota bridge signs
lm.note: In Minnesota, these yellow signs with vertical, black triangles are placed before bridges at most major river crossings and at the beginnings and ends of guardrail sections on large highways.

lm.name: Montana/SD bollard
lm.note:
The most common type of roadside bollard in South Dakota and Montana features a white diamond reflector on top.

Montana tends to have 1 bolt on the reflector, while South Dakota tends to have 2.

NOTE: This is a common design and can be found in many states. Additionally, square bollards can be rotated on their side to look like diamonds. Use with caution.

lm.name: Nevada bollard
lm.note: This bollard is found in Nevada. It consists of a reflector on a thin stick. The reflector is a vertical rectangle that consists of a white field surrounded by a black outline.

lm.name: Saguaro Cactus
lm.note:
In US you can find this cactus(tall,thick upward-curving arms) south of Arizona.

You can find same cactus in Mexico over the border in Sonora or similar one in north of Argentina.

lm.name: Square guardrail
lm.note:
You can find those square guardrails mostly in state of New York and Wyoming.

You can rarely see them in states close to New York state.

lm.name: Washington bollard
lm.note: The state of Washington uses bollards that consist of a white or brown post with a white rectangle on the front of the bollard, and two smaller white or silver squares on the back of the bollard.

lm.name: West Virginia fraction signs
lm.note: West Virginia sometimes features street signs with a symbol that resembles a fraction inside a circle.

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• The US uses yellow middle lines and white outer lines.
  • Double middle lines are the most common.
  • On divided roads, the outer line closest to the median will be yellow, and the other lines will usually be white.

--- NOTE:

  • Double middle lines are less common in Canada, but not rare – use this meta with caution.

lm.name: Roadlines #2
lm.note:
• Interstate highways, US highways, and some state roads have rumble strips in each edge of the road; which are small indentations in the pavement perpendicular to the road.

--- NOTE:

  • Rumble strips may appear in Canada, but are much more rare.

lm.name: California 3 yellow stripes
lm.note: Utility poles in California usually have markings at the bottom of the pole that consist of 3 yellow stripes.

lm.name: horizontal yellow plate
lm.note:
In Utah, Wyoming and southeast Idaho these yellow plates are pretty common.

NOTE: can be found rarely also in Whashington, Oregon and California

lm.name: vertical silver/gold plate
lm.note: In Rhode Island and Massachusetts, you’ll often find silver or gold-colored vertical plates near the base of utility poles.

lm.name: Wisconsin pole sticker
lm.note: A rectangular white metal plate, with an orange rectangle and diamond, can be seen on most poles in Wisconsin and the Michigan peninsula.

lm.name: yellow net
lm.note: In southeastern Pennsylvania, utility poles often have yellow mesh/net near the base.

lm.name: yellow single sticker
lm.note: In newer coverage of Hawaii, you will often see horizontal yellow sticker on poles.

top.html:
The US uses the phrase ‘Speed Limit’ on their speed signs.

The numbers on American speed signs are usually lower than on Canadian ones, since they use miles instead of kilometres. In addition, speed limits ending in 5 are more common in the US.

NOTE: Canada uses the word ‘Maximum’ on their speed signs.
top.raw: The US uses the phrase ‘**Speed Limit**’ on their speed signs. The numbers on American speed signs are usually lower than on Canadian ones, since they use miles instead of kilometres. In addition, speed limits ending in 5 are more common in the US. NOTE: [Canada](https://goo.gl/maps/zVYUCX62g3ENJct2A) uses the word ‘Maximum’ on their speed signs.

top.html:
Road signs in the US tend to use more words compared to their Canadian counterparts. A good example are railway crossing signs, which feature the literal words ‘railroad crossing’ on them. In Canada, these signs are typically blank.

This tendency is also noticeable on yellow diamond warning signs. In Canada, the words will usually be on a rectangular sign below the yellow diamond, which would have a diagram on it instead.
top.raw: Road signs in the US tend to use **more words** compared to their Canadian counterparts. A good example are railway crossing signs, which feature the literal words ‘railroad crossing’ on them. In Canada, these signs are typically blank. This tendency is also noticeable on [yellow diamond warning signs](https://goo.gl/maps/ySfoRRrDjUqSRSub6). In Canada, the words will usually be on a rectangular sign below the yellow diamond, which would have a diagram on it instead.

top.html:
The US uses American English spelling (e.g. center, color).

In addition, the US primarily uses the imperial system for measurements. For example, speed and distance are measured in miles. You will also often see feet and inches on signs, indicating the height of bridges.

NOTE: This is useful to distinguish between the English-speaking parts of Canada, where British English spelling and (usually) the metric system are used. For example, Canada measures speed in kilometres.

For example, speed and distance are measured in **miles**. You will also often see feet and inches on signs, indicating the height of bridges. NOTE: This is useful to distinguish between the English-speaking parts of Canada, where British English spelling and (usually) the [metric system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_system) are used. For example, Canada measures speed in kilometres.

NOTE: Canada uses diamond-shaped junction signs.

top.html:
American yield signs are shaped like an upside-down triangle with a red border, a white field in the middle and the word ‘YIELD’.

NOTE: Canadian yield signs look similar, but lack the ‘YIELD’ text.

top.html:
American one-way signs are usually a horizontal black rectangle with a white arrow inside of it. These signs will also always have the words ‘ONE WAY’ printed on them. In cities, they are a white vertical rectangle with the words ‘ONE WAY’ on them and an arrow underneath.

NOTE: Canadian one-way signs are of the same shape and colour, but might not have the words ‘ONE WAY’ on them.

In cities, they are a white vertical rectangle with the words ‘ONE WAY’ on them and an arrow underneath. NOTE: [Canadian](https://goo.gl/maps/f9n6jHbEQJFrNY5e6) one-way signs are of the same shape and colour, but might not have the words ‘ONE WAY’ on them.

White and orange fibre optic cable markers are almost unique to the US.

NOTE: On very rare occasions, they can be found in Canada.

On divided roads, the outer line closest to the median will be yellow, and the other lines will usually be white.

NOTE: Double middle lines are less common in Canada, but not rare – use this meta with caution. Furthermore, yellow road lines are very rare in Europe.

Interstate highways, US highways, and some state roads have rumble strips on each edge of the road, which are small indentations in the pavement perpendicular to the road. These can be located on the outside edges of the road and in between lanes on multi-lane highways.

NOTE: Rumble strips may appear in Canada, but are much more rare.

top.html:
Small, rectangular manufactured homes, also known as mobile or ‘trailer’ homes, are popular in rural areas of the US. In general, mobile homes are more common in the Southeast, but they can be seen anywhere in the country.

NOTE: This style of home can sometimes be seen in Canada, but to a much lesser extent.

NOTE: Baptist churches are rare in Canada.
